summary: Recommends ways to reduce the forged-origin hijack attack surface by carefully limiting which IP prefixes appear in a Route Origin Authorization (ROA). A key recommendation is to avoid the maxLength attribute in ROAs except in specific cases. It complements RFC 7115 and is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: A permission slip for routes should list exactly what is allowed. Making it too broad lets a cheater slip through, so this says to be specific.

questions: should i use maxlength in roas
how to avoid forged-origin hijacks with rpki
what is a forged-origin sub-prefix hijack
subtitle: Why RPKI route authorizations should list exactly the prefixes you announce, and why maxLength is usually a bad idea.

tldr.problem: A Route Origin Authorization with a maxLength value authorizes many more-specific prefixes than the operator actually announces, and an attacker can forge a route for any of them.
tldr.mechanism: Operators should publish minimal ROAs that list only the prefixes actually originated in BGP, and should avoid maxLength except in a few narrow cases.
tldr.outcome: The tighter ROAs make forged-origin sub-prefix hijacks invalid under route origin validation, at the cost of more operational work when routing changes. This is a Best Current Practice (BCP 185).

today: RFC 9319 is a Best Current Practice published in October 2022. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it complements RFC 7115.

sections.title: The maxLength Problem
sections.content:
The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) uses Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) to map an IP prefix to the Autonomous Systems (ASes) allowed to originate it. A ROA is signed by the party that holds a certificate for the prefixes. The ROA format also has an optional maxLength attribute, a shorthand that authorizes an AS to originate every sub-prefix up to that length.

The catch is that maxLength tends to authorize prefixes that nobody announces. Measurements from June 2017 found that 84% of the prefixes in ROAs using maxLength were vulnerable to a forged-origin sub-prefix hijack. So the RFC says operators SHOULD use minimal ROAs: ROAs that authorize only the prefixes actually originated in BGP, and no others.

The advice complements RFC 7115. It needs no change to the RPKI specifications. The RFC also covers ROAs for DDoS mitigation services and notes how ROAs interact with Remotely Triggered Discard Route (RTDR) filtering.
sections.plainLanguage: A ROA is a signed note saying which network may announce which addresses. A shortcut in the note can accidentally allow far more addresses than you use, and that opens a door for cheaters.

sections.title: The Forged-Origin Sub-Prefix Hijack
sections.content:
The attack matters when the RPKI is deployed, routers use route origin validation to drop invalid routes, but BGPsec (or something like it that checks the AS_PATH) is not deployed. The RFC says this describes a substantial and growing number of large networks at the time of writing.

The running example uses private address space. AS 64496 originates 192.168.0.0/16 and the sub-prefix 192.168.225.0/24. If it publishes the loose ROA (192.168.0.0/16-24, AS 64496), the ROA also covers prefixes it never announces, such as 192.168.0.0/24. A hijacker, AS 64511, announces 192.168.0.0/24 with the path AS 64511, AS 64496, falsely claiming AS 64496 originates it. The route is valid under the ROA. Because longest-prefix-match always prefers the more specific route and no legitimate route to that /24 exists, traffic goes to the hijacker.

With the minimal ROA (192.168.0.0/16, 192.168.225.0/24, AS 64496) the same announcement is invalid: the ROA covers it, but no ROA matches AS 64511 and that prefix. The attacker is left with a forged-origin prefix hijack of the /16. That is less damaging, because AS 64496 still originates the /16 and the hijacker's path is one hop longer.

The RFC's summary: a forged-origin sub-prefix hijack has the same impact as a regular sub-prefix hijack, and it is more damaging than a forged-origin prefix hijack.
sections.plainLanguage: If your slip says you may use a whole street of house numbers but you only live in two houses, a cheater can claim an empty house and everyone sends the mail to them. If the slip lists only your two houses, the cheater's claim is rejected.

sections.title: Recommendations: Minimal ROAs and maxLength
sections.content:
Operators SHOULD use minimal ROAs whenever possible, and SHOULD avoid maxLength because it usually makes a ROA non-minimal. Two exceptions are mentioned. One is when every more-specific prefix permitted by the maxLength value is actually announced by that AS. The other is when the value is much larger than the prefix length and a large number of the more-specific prefixes are announced; the RFC expects that to be rare and calls for operator discretion.

The practice does not need to increase the number of signed ROAs, because a ROA can already hold a list of prefixes. Measurements in June 2017 showed 12% of prefixes in ROAs had a maxLength longer than the prefix length, and 84% of those were non-minimal.

Operators who adopt this and already have published ROAs MUST review them, especially ones using maxLength, replace them as needed, and repeat the review whenever BGP origination or routing policy changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Write down only the addresses you really use. If you have a long list that is mostly all used, a shortcut can be fine, but that is rare.

sections.title: DDoS Mitigation and Ad Hoc Routing Changes
sections.content:
Sometimes a route must be originated at short notice, for example when a DDoS mitigation provider redirects traffic through a scrubbing center. New RPKI objects reach relying parties much more slowly than BGP updates, so the ROA usually has to exist well in advance. Such a ROA is non-minimal, because it lists a prefix that is only sometimes originated.

In that case the ROA SHOULD include only the prefixes always originated and those sometimes originated, and SHOULD NOT include prefixes the operator knows will not be originated. It SHOULD NOT use maxLength unless that changes nothing about the set of included prefixes.

The example has AS 64500 as the mitigation provider for 192.168.0.0/22. A second ROA (192.168.0.0/22, AS 64500) works, but leaves the /22 open to forged-origin sub-prefix hijacks while it is not announced. A variant with 192.168.0.0/22-24 lets AS 64500 attract only the attacked /24, but also exposes the other /24s in the /22 (192.168.1.0/24, 192.168.2.0/24, 192.168.3.0/24).
sections.plainLanguage: If a helper might need to step in during an emergency, they need a permission slip ready in advance. That slip is a bit risky while they are not helping, so keep it as small as you can.

sections.title: Defensive De-aggregation
sections.content:
A victim of a hijack may respond with defensive de-aggregation: announcing more-specific prefixes so they compete with the hijack route in networks that do not do route origin validation. If a path between victim and hijacker includes an AS that filters invalid routes, a minimal ROA can stop those defensive prefixes from reaching networks close to the attacker, weakening the response.

The RFC still recommends minimal ROAs. It gives three reasons: they give the best protection against the attack's immediate impact so the response is less likely to be needed, growing validation adoption will shrink the affected neighborhoods over time, and other measures exist such as direct EBGP adjacencies with networks that would otherwise not see the defensive routes.
sections.plainLanguage: Shouting a more precise address to fight a cheater can be blocked by the rules meant to protect you. The advice is to keep the rules anyway, because they prevent most trouble in the first place.

sections.title: RTDR (Blackhole) Filtering
sections.content:
In destination-based Remotely Triggered Discard Route filtering, very specific prefixes (longer than /24 in IPv4 and longer than /48 in IPv6, possibly even /32 and /128) are announced and tagged with the well-known BGP community from RFC 7999. It is not desirable to put a large maxLength or such specific prefixes into ROAs for this, so route origin validation is a poor fit for RTDR routes. New procedures for that are out of scope.

Operators SHOULD NOT create non-minimal ROAs, by adding ROAs or by using maxLength, to advertise RTDR routes. Operators who let neighbors advertise RTDR routes MUST NOT make creating non-minimal ROAs a prerequisite.
sections.plainLanguage: Emergency blocking notices use very tiny address ranges. Making permission slips for all those tiny ranges would be a mess, so the advice is not to do that.

sections.title: User Interfaces and Operational Trade-offs
sections.content:
Most people create ROAs through a user interface that hides encoding, signing and publishing. Designers and providers of such interfaces SHOULD warn users about the risks of non-minimal ROAs in general and of maxLength in particular. The warnings can be generic, or tailored to the operator's observable BGP routing policy.

The recommendations trade operational agility for security. With minimal ROAs, any change to the set of originated prefixes needs a change to the published ROAs, so procedures may need updating and extra time allowed for propagation. Failing to plan for this could, in the worst case, cause a self-inflicted denial of service. Operators with large allocations and many more-specific announcements are encouraged to automate.
sections.plainLanguage: The forms people use to make these slips should warn them about risky shortcuts. And since the slips must match what you do, you have to update them whenever your plans change.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC makes recommendations about using route origin validation as defined in RFC 6811, and says it introduces no additional security considerations beyond those specified there. It has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: This advice does not add new dangers. It just helps people use the existing safety system more carefully.
